content: The term rhinosinusitis is preferred over sinusitis because inflammation of the sinuses rarely occurs without simultaneous inflammation of the nasal mucosa. Rhinosinusitis is defined as inflammation of both the nasal cavity and the paranasal sinuses. Respiratory tract infections, most commonly colds, can lead to inflammation and thickening of the sinus membranes, which subsequently blocks mucus drainage. These infections can be caused by viruses, bacteria, or fungi. Acute rhinosinusitis (ARS) refers to symptomatic inflammation of the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses that lasts less than four weeks. Acute viral rhinosinusitis (AVRS) typically resolves within 7 to 10 days and is managed symptomatically. Acute bacterial sinusitis, on the other hand, is a complication that arises from a viral upper respiratory infection (URI) or allergic inflammation. Studies have shown that approximately 6% to 7% of children presenting with respiratory symptoms have acute sinusitis. The sinuses located in the forehead (frontal sinuses) do not begin developing until children are between 9 and 12 years old. These sinuses are not fully formed and therefore cannot become infected until the early teenage years. Consequently, headaches related to colds in younger children are usually not due to sinus infections. The most common bacterial pathogens responsible for acute sinusitis include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis. Common Causes of Sinusitis: 1. Viral infections 2. Bacterial infections 3. Fungal infections 4. Allergic sinusitis 5. Nasal polyps 6. Deviated nasal septum 7. Immune system-related diseases that cause nasal blockage 8. Dental infections 9. Aspirin sensitivity 10. Prolonged intubation, which can lead to nosocomial bacterial sinusitis 11. Nasal trauma or injury 12. Presence of a foreign object in the nose 13. Congenital abnormalities, such as cleft palate 14. Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), which can contribute to sinus issues 15. Cystic fibrosis and immunodeficiency syndromes Individuals with immune system problems or antibody deficiencies are at increased risk for developing chronic sinus conditions. Diagnostic and Treatment Guidelines: The diagnostic approach and treatment strategies for rhinosinusitis are typically summarized in clinical algorithms based on established guidelines. These algorithms provide a structured framework for evaluating and managing the condition.
